title: Who Pays for America’s Research and Development?
gist: An infographic explainer tracks the inversion of who funds U.S. research and development since Sputnik: the federal government funded nearly two-thirds in 1957 versus industry's roughly three-quarters today, meaning the Pentagon must now court and adapt commercial innovation rather than drive it.

themes.theme: The great inversion of U.S. R&D funding

insights.claim: When the Soviet Union launched Sputnik in 1957, the U.S. government was the unrivaled patron of American science, funding nearly two-thirds of the nation's research and development, much of it for defense, and for several decades federal dollars pushed the technological frontier while the private sector followed.
insights.speaker: Cogs of War Staff
insights.so_what: Establishes the historical baseline (two-thirds government-funded R&D in the Sputnik era) against which today's inverted funding split should be measured.
insights.quote: It funded nearly two-thirds of the nation\u2019s research and development \u2014 much of it for defense \u2014 defining the early Cold War.
insights.locator: When the Soviet Union launched Sputnik in 1957

insights.claim: Today that arrangement has been inverted: industry now funds roughly three-quarters of U.S. research and development while Washington's share is less than a fifth, meaning the Pentagon must now court and adapt commercial innovation rather than drive it because the cutting edge increasingly emerges from commercial labs.
insights.speaker: Cogs of War Staff
insights.so_what: The central structural finding: with industry now funding ~75% of U.S. R&D versus government's <20%, the Pentagon's role has shifted from R&D driver to R&D adopter, a fundamental change in how defense-tech procurement and partnership strategy should be evaluated.
insights.quote: Today, that arrangement has been inverted. Industry now funds roughly three-quarters of U.S. research and development, while Washington\u2019s share is less than a fifth.
insights.locator: Today, that arrangement has been inverted

insights.claim: The accompanying infographic tracks this funding-source reversal across four snapshots \u2014 1957, 1964, 1980, and 2023, the year with the most current data from the National Science Foundation's National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics.
insights.speaker: Cogs of War Staff
insights.so_what: Identifies the authoritative data source (NSF's NCSES) and the specific benchmark years for anyone wanting to verify or extend the underlying R&D funding-share time series.
insights.locator: Our infographic tracks this reversal across four snapshots

themes.theme: Defense's shrinking share within federal R&D

insights.claim: Defense research and development comprised about 85 percent of total federal R&D funding in the Sputnik era, compared to roughly 49 percent today, though this dynamic reflects less a Pentagon retreat than a surge in civilian funding, mainly National Institutes of Health biomedical research.
insights.speaker: Cogs of War Staff
insights.so_what: Clarifies that defense R&D's declining share of the federal total (85% to 49%) is a relative dilution from NIH biomedical growth, not an absolute Pentagon pullback \u2014 an important distinction for interpreting federal R&D budget trend lines correctly.
insights.quote: Defense research and development comprised about 85 percent of total funding in the Sputnik era, compared to roughly 49 percent today.
insights.locator: The infographic\u2019s second layer also explores

insights.claim: If the funding lens is narrowed specifically to engineering research, the Defense Department remains the dominant funder, despite defense's declining share of total federal R&D once biomedical research is included.
insights.speaker: Cogs of War Staff
insights.so_what: Signals that within engineering disciplines specifically \u2014 as opposed to R&D broadly \u2014 the Pentagon retains outsized funding influence, relevant for engineering-focused defense contractors and universities assessing their federal funding exposure.
insights.locator: However, this dynamic reflects less a Pentagon retreat

themes.theme: Who performs R&D versus who funds it

insights.claim: Measured by who performs research and development rather than who funds it, industry's share is larger still at about 77 percent in 2023, because companies also carry out federally funded work under contract.
insights.speaker: Cogs of War Staff
insights.so_what: Distinguishes funding source from performance location: industry actually performs 77% of all U.S. R&D (higher than its ~75% funding share) because it also executes government-funded contract work, reinforcing that commercial labs are now the physical locus of American innovation.
insights.quote: Measured by performance, industry\u2019s share is larger still (about 77 percent in 2023), because companies also carry out federally funded work under contract.
insights.locator: Although we didn\u2019t discuss who performs research
